doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: State of jazz today and a European tour with Peanuts Hucko
summary: Marty feels jazz needs exposure and tells of a Portuguese audience that cheered the Hucko Armstrong tribute band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Very quickly, what’s your take on the state of jazz today?

Jazz is alive I love it. There’s nothing wrong with jazz, it’s just we’re not getting enough exposure to the people. Because not enough radio stations play it, and like you get KCR and BGO, they’re playing some far out jazz that a lot of people don’t really like to listen to. So that’s my personal feeling. Because sometimes I listen to those stations and I don’t really like what I hear. Because I’m from the old jazz, you know, like Bunny Berigan, guys like this. And I love jazz, but when I listen to some of those things, you know when they do these free for all things, it just turns me off, I just don’t like it. So I feel if I don’t like it and I’m a musician, can you imagine the average lay person who listens and says what the hell is that?

Yeah, what is that? So I feel sad because you know how I know there’s a market for it? I went to Europe about five years in a row with Peanuts Hucko. We were doing a tribute to Louis Armstrong. We had Peanuts, Trummy Young, Billy Butterfield, Jack Lesberg and Gus Johnson. When I tell you we went to Portugal for one night, and we played opposite a kid who was a local hero, who had a hit record, he was about 23 years old, and he was fantastic. He had all kinds of amplifiers. Three guys they sounded like a whole orchestra. It was great. And he had a hit record and he was from that town, and they loved him. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -38-

we had to follow him. So now he breaks it up, I mean completely. Now to introduce us and we come out, and we get [sparse applause]. We started to play “Back Home Again Indiana,” well you never heard anything like that in your whole life. Clomping, Stamping, Cheering, Whistling, “hey you guys are great man.” They went crazy. We tore it up. We had to do four encores, they wouldn’t let us off the stage. I said man this is fantastic. These six old guys come on here and they say what’s going on. I was with the world’s greatest band too, the world’s greatest. Joe Muranyi. Everybody in the band was great. People loved it. They were swinging. I mean when the band is swinging it gets to the people, I don’t care what you say.
